records.title: What the original questions ask you to separate
paragraphs: Workbook questions 1, 3 and 9 ask for a connected cause-and-conditions explanation. A microorganism must be present for its population to grow. Suitable nutrients, moisture, temperature and time can affect growth; a warm hamburger does not create bacteria from nothing. Name each condition, then explain how it changes the possible exposure.

Questions 2a–b ask about Robert Koch and Louis Pasteur. Koch helped establish links between particular microbes and particular diseases through testable evidence. Pasteur showed that heating can reduce microbes in foods and beverages and helped challenge spontaneous-generation explanations. Their work supports a method: identify an agent, test a pathway, and compare alternatives.
records.task: Use workbook Chapter 9 questions 1, 2a–b, 3 and 9. Write a cause-and-conditions explanation for the hamburger. Include Koch's and Pasteur's different contributions and one observation that would test your claim.
records.model: A pathogen in the food, if present, could multiply with suitable moisture, nutrients, temperature and time. Koch's approach asks for evidence linking a particular organism to illness; Pasteur's heating work supports a way to reduce microbes. Compare exposed and unexposed food and people before naming the cause.

records.title: Identify the organism before choosing a control
paragraphs: Workbook questions 4–8 deliberately mix categories. A bacterium is a cell that can divide in suitable conditions. A virus requires a host cell to produce new virus particles. Giardia is a protist associated with contaminated water; athlete's foot is a fungal infection. These differences change the evidence and prevention pathway.

The workbook's older phrase “AIDS virus” refers to HIV. HIV transmission requires specific exposure to infected body fluids; casual proximity is not a route. Use a transmission chain for each example: source, exit, transfer, entry and susceptible host. A label alone is not an explanation.
records.task: For workbook Chapter 9 questions 4–8, make a four-row comparison of bacterium, virus, Giardia and athlete's-foot fungus. For each, give the category, one plausible route of exposure and one prevention action tied to that route.
records.model: For example, Giardia is a protist that can be swallowed in contaminated untreated water, so treating drinking water interrupts the route. A cold virus replicates in host cells and can spread through respiratory exposure; an antibiotic does not directly stop that replication.

records.title: Separate transmission from unequal exposure
paragraphs: Workbook questions 10–13 contrast communicable infections with non-communicable conditions. A disease classification says whether an infectious agent can pass between hosts; it does not say whether a person is responsible for illness. Clean water, safe food handling and sanitation reduce some transmission routes, while genetics, behaviour and environment can affect non-communicable risk.

Questions 14–15 use an older rich-country/poor-country comparison. Poverty can change exposure, nutrition, housing and access to prevention or care; it is not itself a pathogen. Mortality patterns vary by place and time, so use the source as a historical comparison rather than a current ranking or a claim about an individual.
records.task: Use workbook Chapter 9 questions 10–15 to build two columns: infectious route and non-communicable risk. Then explain how one social condition changes exposure or access without blaming an affected person.
records.model: Crowded housing can make some respiratory exposures more likely, while limited access to care can delay treatment. Neither condition identifies a specific pathogen. A non-communicable condition can involve inherited, environmental and other factors without person-to-person transmission.

records.title: Ten preservation methods, several mechanisms
paragraphs: Workbook question 16 names drying, canning, salting, smoking, refrigeration, freezing, chemical additives, vacuum packing, irradiation and pasteurization. Sort them by what they change. Drying and salting reduce available water; refrigeration and freezing slow growth; canning and pasteurization use heat; vacuum packing changes oxygen exposure; irradiation and approved additives can reduce microbes or slow spoilage. Smoking combines effects and does not guarantee safety by itself.

Question 17 asks for five ways to protect surfaces and utensils. Clean hands and food-contact surfaces, separate raw from ready-to-eat foods, use separate or thoroughly cleaned tools, prevent drips from raw foods, and follow current cooking/chilling guidance. Explain which transfer pathway each action interrupts.
records.task: Complete workbook Chapter 9 questions 16–17. Group all ten named preservation methods by mechanism, then choose five surface or utensil controls and state the contamination route each prevents.
records.model: Refrigeration slows many microbes but does not sterilize food. Pasteurization applies controlled heat to reduce targeted hazards. A separate board for raw meat prevents transfer to ready-to-eat vegetables; washing and sanitizing the board before reuse addresses the same route.

records.title: A clean surface is not the same as a sterile instrument
paragraphs: Workbook questions 2c–d connect Florence Nightingale's sanitation work and Joseph Lister's antiseptic surgery to reduced infection. The point is a change in the exposure pathway, not a promise that every hospital infection disappeared.

Questions 18–20 distinguish antiseptics used on appropriate living tissue, disinfectants used on surfaces, sterilization intended to eliminate viable microorganisms on equipment, and aseptic practices that keep a procedure from introducing contamination. The older textbook loosely calls some disinfecting “sterilizing”; keep the terms separate. Examples include hand hygiene, appropriate sterile instruments, clean barriers and safe handling of dressings.
records.task: For workbook Chapter 9 questions 18–20, plan a safe preparation sequence. Name where an antiseptic, a surface disinfectant, sterile equipment and an aseptic handling step belong, then explain the failure if one is omitted.
records.model: A surface disinfectant belongs on the preparation surface as directed, not in a wound. Sterile equipment and clean handling reduce transfer into vulnerable tissue. Hand hygiene and suitable barriers support aseptic technique; a neat-looking room alone is not proof of sterility.

records.title: Read the historical disease table as evidence
paragraphs: Workbook Chapter 10 questions 1–5 introduce shared responsibility, pandemic scale and the harm of introduced diseases to First Nations. The historical impact was intensified by colonization, displacement and disrupted access to resources and care. Do not explain it as an inherent weakness of a people. Distinguish a pathogen's spread from the social conditions that changed exposure and response.

Question 6 asks for a four-disease table: bubonic plague, tuberculosis, 1918 influenza and HIV/AIDS. For each, separate the time/place, social conditions and impact. These events differ in pathogen, route and historical context. A pandemic label describes geographic spread over time; it does not tell you the organism or severity for every person.
records.task: Complete the four-column workbook Chapter 10 question 6 table. For each disease, record a dated place, a social condition that affected spread, an impact and one source limitation; then answer questions 1–5 with the same cause-versus-context care.
records.model: For 1918 influenza, a respiratory virus spread across countries during a period of mass movement. Crowding and limited treatment options affected impact. A historical mortality figure needs a source and date; it does not describe a current local risk.

records.title: Public health uses more than one control
paragraphs: Workbook questions 7–11 ask why communities acted and what public agencies do for water, garbage and human or animal waste. Use a source-to-tap account: protect the source, treat water, monitor the system, communicate results and correct failures. Landfill containment and wastewater treatment reduce routes from waste to water; a liner or one clean sample is not a complete guarantee. Agency names and responsibilities in the older book reflect its publication date.

Question 12 uses the textbook's old 0–100 Air Quality Index. Read it as a historical source, then use a current local Air Quality Health Index notice for present advice. Question 13 asks for six diseases from the textbook's vaccination examples; use the printed page for that exercise, and use the current Alberta schedule for today's program. Question 14 calls the food campaign “BAC”; the printed figure gives its four actions: Clean, Cook, Separate and Chill. Each interrupts a different food-safety pathway.
records.task: Use workbook Chapter 10 questions 7–14. Draw a source-to-tap control chain, explain waste and air alerts, then identify six textbook vaccine examples and the four food-safety actions. Mark which details are historical and where you would check today's Alberta guidance.
records.model: Source protection, treatment, distribution monitoring and a public advisory are separate safeguards. The old AQI bands do not set today's AQHI advice. The textbook lists several vaccine-preventable diseases, while current schedules are maintained by Alberta Health. Clean, Cook, Separate and Chill address different contamination and growth routes.

records.title: A risk table needs an action and an evidence limit
paragraphs: Workbook question 15 is a factor–concern–control table. Population crowding, migration, restaurants, travel, food supply and sexual activity or childbirth do not all share one route. Complete each row with the specific concern and a proportionate public-health control, such as monitoring, inspection, safe transport, education or access to care.

Question 16 asks whether guidelines matter; answer with a concrete benefit and a limit, not a slogan. Question 17 refers to a Walkerton timeline on printed textbook page 186, which is missing from this supplied PDF. The workbook prompt remains available, but the absent timeline cannot support a claim about criminal liability. Use the source material your teacher supplies before making a legal judgment.
records.task: Complete workbook Chapter 10 questions 15–17. Fill three contrasting factor–concern–control rows and justify a public guideline. For the Walkerton prompt, list the timeline evidence needed before assigning responsibility and identify the page missing from this PDF.
records.model: Restaurant inspection addresses food handling; disease monitoring addresses a different community risk. A guideline can reduce preventable exposure but needs clear communication and follow-through. A criminal-charge conclusion cannot be supported from a timeline that is absent from the provided textbook.

records.title: Read the physical-defence chart as a route map
paragraphs: Workbook Chapter 11 questions 2–4 ask you to fill a structure–function chart, not memorize a single “first line.” Skin is a physical and chemical barrier; mucus traps particles; cilia help move mucus; tears wash the eye; stomach acid reduces some swallowed microbes. Eyelids, hair and other structures contribute in different places. Match each structure to the entry route it protects.

The smoking-and-cough question asks about damaged airway clearance. Smoke exposure can impair cilia and irritate airways, so coughing may increase. It does not prove one person's cough has only that cause. Use the chart to explain the mechanism without diagnosing a classmate.
records.task: Complete the original workbook Chapter 11 physical-defence chart on page 19. For at least six structures, state the entry route, the barrier action and what might happen if that defence is damaged; include the smoking/cough question with a limit on diagnosis.
records.model: Cilia move mucus and trapped particles away from deeper airways. When clearance is impaired, particles and mucus can linger and coughing can increase. A cough can also have other causes, so this mechanism is not an individual diagnosis.

records.title: Put the immune events in a defensible order
paragraphs: Workbook questions 5–9 move from inflammation and macrophages toward targeted defence. A sliver damages tissue; blood flow and vessel changes can make the area red, warm and swollen while immune cells respond. Macrophages can engulf material, but swelling alone does not identify a pathogen.

Questions 10–13 ask you to recognize antigens and order a simplified five-stage response. The workbook sequence places bacterial entry and engulfment before antigen presentation, helper-cell signalling, B-cell antibody production and memory. Real immune responses have overlapping pathways; the five cards are a teaching model. Antigens may be on pathogens or other cells, so do not mark every normal body cell as a foreign threat.
records.task: Use workbook Chapter 11 questions 5–13. Order the five response cards on page 21, explain the sliver example, and justify two of the antigen-scenario choices using self-versus-foreign context.
records.model: A possible teaching order is entry/engulfment, displayed antigen, helper-cell signalling, B-cell antibody response with other immune cells, then memory. These events overlap in real life. Redness after a sliver reflects inflammation, not proof of a named infection.

records.title: Compare the source's immunity diagrams and cases
paragraphs: Workbook questions 14–16 ask for an immunity flowchart and classification. Active immunity follows the person's own response after infection or vaccination; passive immunity comes from supplied antibodies, such as certain maternal transfers or an antitoxin. Passive protection can act quickly but does not create the same person's immune memory.

Questions 17–22 extend the model to blood compatibility, vaccines, antitoxin and allergies. O-negative red cells are often described as universal donor red cells, but transfusion compatibility still needs clinical testing and context. A vaccine is designed to train immune recognition; an antitoxin supplies antibodies. The older book's vaccine list is historical, and an allergy is an immune response to a usually harmless substance.
records.task: Complete workbook Chapter 11 questions 14–22. Draw active and passive branches with an example of each, then compare vaccine with antitoxin and qualify the O-negative donor statement. Use the original page for every case.
records.model: Vaccination is active because the recipient develops a response and memory; supplied antitoxin is passive because antibodies are transferred. O-negative red cells can be compatible in many emergency red-cell contexts, but crossmatching and clinical rules still matter.

records.title: Match a medicine to its target and instructions
paragraphs: Workbook question 1 asks where penicillin originated: it was discovered from Penicillium mould. Questions 23–25 distinguish symptom-relief medicines from antibiotics, explain why antibiotics do not directly work on a viral cold, and ask about resistance and adverse effects. Bacteria, not the person, evolve resistance under selection pressure.

Questions 26–27 ask for safe use and label reading. The right choice depends on the medicine, instructions, allergies, interactions and current clinical advice. An over-the-counter label should be read for purpose, dose, warnings and interactions. These classroom examples support reasoning and do not prescribe treatment for an individual.
records.task: For workbook Chapter 11 questions 1 and 23–27, compare an antibiotic with a symptom-relief product. State each target, a reason it might be inappropriate, and three label or clinician-instruction checks.
records.model: An antibiotic targets susceptible bacteria and does not directly treat a viral cold. A pain reliever may reduce a symptom without removing its cause. The user should follow the actual label and clinician or pharmacist advice, including dose and interaction warnings.

records.title: Use the original karyotypes, not a guessed count
paragraphs: Workbook Chapter 12 questions 1–3 locate chromosomes in the nucleus, test DNA base pairing and ask for the common human chromosome count. For the printed A–G–C–T–G strand, the complementary strand is T–C–G–A–C. Most human body cells have 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 pairs, but the model has exceptions.

Question 4 contains three image-based karyotypes: identify the extra chromosome 21, single X and XXY patterns from the actual images rather than the names printed beside the question. Questions 5–6 use the common XX/XY school model; do not infer a person's gender identity or every biological variation from those letters.
records.task: Open workbook Chapter 12 pages 27–28. Write the complementary DNA bases, count one karyotype's key chromosome difference, and justify each of the three image-based identifications using the shown chromosomes.
records.model: A pairs with T and G with C, giving T–C–G–A–C. Trisomy 21 has three copies of chromosome 21; a single X and XXY are distinct chromosome patterns. The original image must be read to match each numbered karyotype.

records.title: Show the boxes, then state what they predict
paragraphs: Workbook question 7 names Mendel's pea-plant work. Question 8 is a heterozygous tall plant crossed with a short plant: write Tt × tt, put T and t across one edge and t and t along the other, then fill Tt, tt, Tt and tt. The 1:1 ratio is a probability under the model, not a guaranteed result for four plants.

Question 9 uses a simplified brown/blue eye model; real eye colour involves multiple genes, so use its BB × bb exercise only as a classroom one-gene model. Question 10 asks for Ww × Ww white-wool sheep, a genotype/phenotype table and a 3:1 model ratio. Explain why a box represents a possibility, not an actual offspring's measured genotype.
records.task: Draw and label the three original Chapter 12 crosses on workbook pages 29–30. For each, show parental alleles, gametes, all four cells, genotype probability and phenotype probability; label the eye-colour assumption as simplified.
records.model: Tt × tt gives two Tt and two tt boxes, a model 1:1 phenotype ratio if T is dominant. Ww × Ww gives WW, Ww, Ww and ww, or three white to one black in the simple model. Actual small families may differ.

records.title: Keep the Q11 and Q12 pedigrees separate
paragraphs: Workbook Q11 on p. 31 asks learners to read generations, shaded names and Jim’s children from a named family pedigree. The printed textbook p. 218 cited by the workbook is absent from the supplied textbook PDF, so the complete workbook figure remains visible.

Workbook Q12 on p. 32 has its own pedigree. Two unaffected parents have an affected child, which supports a recessive interpretation in the intended simple model. Q13 then asks learners to construct a new pedigree from the Pederson family description.
records.task: Use original workbook pp. 31–33. Answer Q11 only from the p. 31 family figure; answer Q12 from the separate p. 32 figure; construct Q13 with a legend and label its human eye-colour rule as simplified.
records.model: Q11: three generations; Sue, Joe, Jim and Tim are shaded; Jim has Tim and Lori. Q12: two unaffected parents have an affected child, supporting recessive inheritance in the intended simple model. Q13 needs a legend and correct family connections.

records.title: A DNA change, its cause and its effect are different claims
paragraphs: Workbook questions 14–15 ask how copying can change DNA and what a mutagen is. A mutation is a sequence or chromosome change; a mutagen is an exposure that can increase the chance of some changes. A change can be neutral, harmful or occasionally beneficial, and an acquired change in body cells is not automatically passed to children.

Question 16 asks about alcohol or drug exposure during pregnancy. Discuss possible fetal risk without blaming individuals or treating every substance and dose as identical. Question 17 raises amniocentesis ethics: distinguish procedure risk, information gained, consent and what choices a family may or may not make. Follow current medical guidance for personal decisions.
records.task: Use workbook Chapter 12 questions 14–17. Build a claim–mechanism–uncertainty table for DNA copying error, one mutagen exposure and prenatal exposure; then write an amniocentesis decision frame with benefits, risks and consent.
records.model: A copying error can change a DNA sequence; a mutagen may increase the probability of certain changes, but an exposure does not prove an individual's outcome. Prenatal health decisions need current clinical advice. Amniocentesis is an informed-choice question, not a compulsory conclusion.

records.title: Judge research by evidence, consent and alternatives
paragraphs: Workbook question 18 asks for benefits and concerns of genetic research. Use specific possible benefits, such as understanding a disease mechanism, alongside limitations, privacy, unequal access and potential misuse. A research finding does not automatically become an approved treatment.

Question 19 proposes cloning people to harvest organs. Treat the premise as an ethics hypothetical, not a current clinical option. Consider the clone as a person with rights and consent, identify harms and uncertainty, and compare alternatives such as donation and research that does not create a person for parts.
records.task: Complete workbook Chapter 12 questions 18–19. Fill a two-column benefit/concern chart with evidence and limits, then write a consent-and-rights response to the cloning hypothetical that considers at least one alternative.
records.model: Genetic research can help explain a disease or guide some care, but evidence, privacy and access matter. Creating a person for organ harvesting would violate that person's autonomy; the classroom argument must address rights and alternatives rather than treating a clone as equipment.
